Reproducing Henry & Kohn (2022) from CRCNS v4-2¶

Paper. Henry CA, Kohn A (2022). Feature representation under crowding in macaque V1 and V4 neuronal populations. Current Biology 32, 5126-5137. doi:10.1016/j.cub.2022.10.049. The claims file claims/henry-2022.yaml was written from the version of record (main text, STAR Methods and Supplemental Information, as extracted from the PDF).

Dataset. CRCNS v4-2, "Simultaneous extracellular recordings from visual areas V1 and V4 from macaque monkeys viewing crowded displays" (doi:10.6080/K0736P4H), the paper's deposit. Files are streamed from the public S3 bucket crcnsarchive under v4-2/live/; the zip is opened in place and nothing is written to disk.

Version. CRCNS data sets are not versioned (docs/archives.md), and the paper cites the data set by its DOI only, so the version pinned is the one published under v4-2/live/ (the bucket holds no other), recorded as unversioned. Its data description is version 0.7 (9 Nov 2022). The MD5 sums from the data set's checksums.md5 for the files read are: data.zip bdd60f999b997523151b9ae24a42b837 (checked against the bytes read, below) and docs/crcns_v4-2_data_description.pdf 40f2f30456a87ad3999e8a929a424220.

What the data set holds. Spike counts (0 to 0.25 s after each stimulus onset) of the populations analysed in the paper: the separation experiment (11 sessions, 22 populations per area, 396 V1 and 691 V4 units) and the distractor-orientation experiment (4 sessions, Figure 6E). It holds no receptive-field mapping sessions, no per-session coarse mapping of targets and single distractors, and no waveforms.

The pseudo-population analysis (figs3-pseudo-populations) is in the second notebook, pseudo_populations.ipynb, to keep each notebook within the run time limit.

Method details the claims file leaves to the paper are cited in the helper crowding.py and in each section. All analyses use every deposited unit: the deposit holds exactly the paper's 396 and 691 units, and the selection rule of the Methods does not regenerate them (data-populations).

import crowding as cw

T0 = time.time()
print(cw.DATASET)
D = cw.load()
print("MD5 of data.zip as read:", D["md5"], "; checksums.md5 gives", cw.DATA_MD5,
      "; match:", D["md5"] == cw.DATA_MD5)
S, O = D["separation"], D["orientation"]
SP = cw.SPACINGS
SPL = {1.32: "1.3", 1.64: "1.6", 2.04: "2.1", 2.56: "2.6"}
AREAS = ("V1", "V4")


def pops(area, exp=None):
    return [p for p in (exp or S) if p["area"] == area]


def ttest_1s_greater(a, b, equal_var=True):
    return stats.ttest_ind(a, b, equal_var=equal_var, alternative="greater")

Separation experiment, epochs per stimulus condition: min 19 median 44.0 max 54
Spike counts: integers from 0 to 56 spikes per 0.25 s epoch

The description says 15 sessions in two files, populations per area and orientation range, spike counts per stimulus epoch (neurons x epochs) and fields for session and animal; the values agree: 11 sessions (7 from AL, 4 from CA) and 22 populations per area in the separation file, 4 sessions (2 per animal) and 8 populations per area in the orientation file. The paper's design is there: four target orientations at -9, -3, +3 and +9 degrees from the reference, isolated or with four distractors at +/-10 degrees alternating around the target, at four spacings (stored as 1.32, 1.64, 2.04 and 2.56 degrees, printed in the paper as 1.3, 1.6, 2.1 and 2.6), and two references 90 degrees apart per session. The files also hold blank epochs and distractor-only epochs, which the description does not mention; blank epochs are taken as the spontaneous condition. The orientation experiment has seven target orientations (-12 to +12 degrees in steps of 4), alone or with one of two distractor configurations whose orientations are swapped (+10/-10 against -10/+10), at one spacing that the file does not state.

# Are the V1 and V4 epochs of a population the same epochs in the same order?
rows = []
for a, b in zip(pops("V1"), pops("V4")):
    ka = a["p"].fillna(-1).groupby(["kind", "oi", "sep"]).size()
    kb = b["p"].fillna(-1).groupby(["kind", "oi", "sep"]).size()
    same_seq = (a["p"].fillna(-1)[["kind", "oi", "sep"]].values == b["p"].fillna(-1)[["kind", "oi", "sep"]].values).all(1)
    rows.append(dict(session=a["session"], orange=a["orange"], epochs=len(a["p"]),
                     same_counts_per_condition=ka.equals(kb), same_condition_at_same_index=same_seq.mean()))
al = pd.DataFrame(rows)
print(al.to_string())
print("Expected share of equal conditions at the same index if orders were unrelated: about",
      round(float(np.mean([(p["p"].fillna(-1).groupby(["kind", "oi", "sep"]).size() / len(p["p"])).pow(2).sum()
                           for p in pops("V1")])), 3))


def resid_series(p):
    """Population mean count per epoch minus the mean of its condition."""
    c = p["counts"].astype(float)
    key = p["p"].kind + p["p"].oi.astype(str) + p["p"].sep.fillna(-1).astype(str)
    r = c.copy()
    for k in key.unique():
        m = (key == k).values
        r[:, m] = c[:, m] - c[:, m].mean(1, keepdims=True)
    return r.mean(0)


def lagcorr(x, lag):
    return np.corrcoef(x[:-lag], x[lag:])[0, 1]


rows = []
for p in S:
    x = resid_series(p)
    rows.append(dict(area=p["area"], session=p["session"], orange=p["orange"],
                     lag1=lagcorr(x, 1), lag10=lagcorr(x, 10), lag50=lagcorr(x, 50),
                     pair_even=np.corrcoef(x[0:-1:2], x[1::2])[0, 1],
                     pair_odd=np.corrcoef(x[1:-1:2], x[2::2])[0, 1]))
ac = pd.DataFrame(rows)
print()
print("Autocorrelation of the population residual over the stored epoch order (median over populations):")
print(ac.groupby("area")[["lag1", "lag10", "lag50", "pair_even", "pair_odd"]].median().round(3).to_string())
print("Populations with lag-10 autocorrelation above 0.1: V1", int((ac.query("area=='V1'").lag10 > 0.1).sum()),
      "of 22, V4", int((ac.query("area=='V4'").lag10 > 0.1).sum()), "of 22")

Within each session and orientation range the V1 and V4 entries have the same number of epochs of every condition, but not in the same order: the share of epochs whose condition agrees at the same index is at the level expected for unrelated orders. The V1 epochs carry slow fluctuations of the population response (residual autocorrelation at a lag of 10 epochs), as recordings in time order do; the V4 epochs carry none. So the V1 epochs are consistent with the recording order and the V4 epochs are stored in some other order, and epochs cannot be matched between the areas. No claim tested here pairs V1 and V4 epochs. The two epochs of one trial cannot be told apart: in V1 the residuals of epochs 2k and 2k+1 are no more alike than those of 2k+1 and 2k+2. The description says nothing about either point.

# Clock check: the counts must follow the stimulus labels. Contrast target-alone with blank epochs,
# with the true labels and with the labels shifted by one and by five epochs.
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
rows = []
for p in S:
    kind = p["p"].kind.values
    for shift in (0, 1, 5):
        k = np.roll(kind, shift)
        d = p["counts"][:, k == "alone"].mean(1) - p["counts"][:, k == "blank"].mean(1)
        rows.append(dict(area=p["area"], shift=shift, mean_diff=d.mean(), frac_pos=(d > 0).mean()))
ck = pd.DataFrame(rows).groupby(["area", "shift"]).agg(mean_alone_minus_blank=("mean_diff", "mean"),
                                                      frac_neurons_alone_above_blank=("frac_pos", "mean"))
print(ck.round(3).to_string())
# Orientation labels: single-neuron AUC between the extreme orientations, true against shifted labels
rows = []
for p in S:
    oi = p["p"].oi.values.copy()
    kind = p["p"].kind.values
    for shift in (0, 1):
        o = np.roll(oi, shift)
        a = p["counts"][:, (kind == "alone") & (o == 0)]
        b = p["counts"][:, (kind == "alone") & (o == 3)]
        au = np.array([cw.auc(a[i], b[i]) for i in range(a.shape[0])])
        rows.append(dict(area=p["area"], shift=shift, mean_abs_auc_dev=np.mean(np.abs(au - 0.5))))
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).groupby(["area", "shift"]).mean_abs_auc_dev.mean().round(3).to_string())

Responses follow the labels: with the true labels target-alone counts exceed blank counts, and the extreme orientations are told apart more than with labels shifted by one epoch, in both areas. With the labels shifted the target and blank difference vanishes. The labels and counts share one order within each area. The next cell breaks this down by population.

# Blank and distractor-only epochs against target epochs, per population: mean over neurons of
# (mean count - blank mean) / blank SD, and the orientation tuning of target-alone counts (mean
# over neurons of the variance of the four orientation means over the mean within-orientation
# variance of a mean; about 1 without tuning), with true labels and labels shifted by one epoch.
rows = []
for p in S:
    c, P = p["counts"], p["p"]
    bl = c[:, cw.stim_mask(p, "blank")]
    sd = bl.std(1, ddof=1)
    sd[sd == 0] = 1
    r = dict(area=p["area"], animal=p["animal"], session=p["session"], orange=p["orange"], blank_mean=bl.mean())
    for kind, s, lab in (("alone", None, "z_alone"), ("dist", None, "z_dist_only"), ("crowd", 1.32, "z_crowd_1.3")):
        r[lab] = np.mean((c[:, cw.stim_mask(p, kind, s)].mean(1) - bl.mean(1)) / sd)
    for shift in (0, 1):
        kind = np.roll(P.kind.values, shift)
        oi = np.roll(P.oi.values, shift)
        ms = [(kind == "alone") & (oi == o) for o in range(4)]
        means = np.stack([c[:, m].mean(1) for m in ms], 1)
        within = np.mean([c[:, m].var(1) / m.sum() for m in ms], 0)
        r[f"tuning_F_shift{shift}"] = np.nanmean(means.var(1, ddof=1) / within)
    rows.append(r)
BL = pd.DataFrame(rows)
print(BL.round(2).to_string())
flat = BL.groupby("session").z_alone.max() < 0.5
print("Sessions whose target epochs do not exceed the blank epochs (z < 0.5 in every population):",
      list(flat[flat].index))

In sessions 1, 2 and 8 to 11 (12 of the 22 populations in each area, both animals) the epochs labelled blank (target and distractor contrast 0) and those labelled distractor-only give the same counts as the target epochs (z near 0), while in sessions 3 to 7 the targets drive the neurons well above the blank epochs. The labels are aligned with the counts in all sessions: target-alone counts depend on the target orientation with the true labels (tuning F above 1) and not with labels shifted by one epoch. The contrast parameters hold the same two values (0 and 0.5) for targets and distractors in every session, so nothing in the labels marks the six sessions as different; only the counts do. In sessions 3 to 7 every unit's target-alone mean exceeds its blank mean; in the other six sessions 8% to 86% of V1 units and 23% to 75% of V4 units do, around the half expected when the two kinds of epoch do not differ. So in six sessions the epochs labelled blank cannot have been blank, or their counts are not those of the epochs the labels describe; the files cannot tell which. Spontaneous activity cannot be measured there. This is recorded as a finding; it bears on the selection rule (data-populations) and on the driven fractions of figs6-common-neuron-pool.

data-populations¶

Eleven sessions gave 22 neuronal populations in each area, of on average 19 +/- 1.9 V1 neurons and 31 +/- 3.4 V4 neurons, 396 V1 and 691 V4 neurons in the single-neuron analyses.

The selection rule ("responses >= 1 s.d. above spontaneous rate", STAR Methods) is applied to the deposited units under the two readings of the criterion, with blank epochs as the spontaneous condition (the only spontaneous data held) and the SD over blank epochs.

Result: partially reproduced. The data set holds 11 sessions and 22 populations per area, and its units number exactly 396 in V1 and 691 in V4 (264 and 132, 288 and 403 per animal, as in Figure S7), with mean population sizes of 18.0 +/- 1.7 and 31.4 +/- 3.4, within tolerance. But the deposited units are the selected ones, and the Methods' rule, applied to them under either reading of the criterion, keeps only 115 or 133 of the V1 units and 147 or 174 of the V4 units, far from the reported counts. One reason is in the data check: in sessions 1, 2 and 8 to 11 the epochs labelled blank respond as the target epochs do, so no unit there passes. The counts hold for the data as deposited; the stated selection does not regenerate them.

Single-neuron discriminability (Figure 2A to 2C)¶

fig2a-v1-single-neuron-near: V1 single-neuron discriminability of target orientation is lower with the nearest distractors than for targets alone, with a regression slope of 0.60 (95% CI 0.50 to 0.69).

fig2b-v4-single-neuron-near: In V4 the loss of single-neuron discriminability with the nearest distractors is stronger, with a regression slope of 0.20 (95% CI 0.14 to 0.26).

fig2c-farthest-spacing-slopes: At the farthest spacing ... slopes of 0.74 (0.66 to 0.82) in V1 and 0.44 (0.37 to 0.50) in V4.

fig2c-v4-worse-all-spacings: Distractors impair single-neuron discriminability more in V4 than in V1 at every target-distractor spacing.

All deposited units are used (n = 396 and 691, as in Figure 2). AUC of the two extreme target orientations, the one closer to 0 degrees taken as the preferred (Results, paragraph on Figure 2A); OLS slope of crowded on target-alone AUC; 95% CI from 1000 bootstrap samples over neurons. "Closer to 0" is read as the axial orientation; in the paper's frame of orientations relative to the reference (-9 to +9 degrees) the two extremes are equally close to 0, so the reading with the lower orientation always taken as preferred is shown as a variant (slope_lower_orientation_first).

Result: fig2a-v1-single-neuron-near reproduced. The V1 slope at 1.3 degrees is 0.580 (95% CI 0.486 to 0.669), within 0.60 +/- 0.10, with the CI below 1; 0.607 through (0.5, 0.5). With the lower orientation always preferred the slopes are 0.602 and 0.200 at 1.3 degrees and 0.742 and 0.440 at 2.6 (V1 and V4), within 0.022 of the main reading, so no outcome below depends on it.

Result: fig2b-v4-single-neuron-near reproduced. The V4 slope at 1.3 degrees is 0.206 (0.145 to 0.269), within 0.20 +/- 0.06.

Result: fig2c-farthest-spacing-slopes reproduced. At 2.6 degrees the slopes are 0.728 (0.647 to 0.798) in V1 and 0.437 (0.368 to 0.501) in V4, within 0.74 +/- 0.08 and 0.44 +/- 0.07.

Result: fig2c-v4-worse-all-spacings reproduced. At every spacing the V4 slope is below the V1 slope and the two 95% CIs do not overlap (reading b). Per animal the V4 slope is below the V1 slope at every spacing in both animals (AL 0.319 to 0.514 against 0.490 to 0.582; CA 0.122 to 0.379 against 0.644 to 0.874).

fig3ab-correlations-reduced¶

Distractors reduce noise correlations, from 0.07 +/- 0.003 to 0.05 +/- 0.002 in V1 and from 0.11 +/- 0.001 to 0.06 +/- 0.001 in V4 with the nearest distractors (paired t test, p < 0.001).

Pairs within each population; per stimulus, trials with both counts within 3 SD of their means; averaged over the four target orientations (STAR Methods). Reading (a), every stored epoch as a presentation, is the only one that can be run: the files do not say which epoch of a trial is the first, and the residuals do not reveal the pairing (data check), so reading (b) cannot be formed.

Fano factors (Figure 3D and 3E)¶

fig3d-v1-fano-closest: In V1, distractors at the closest spacing slightly reduce variability, the Fano factor falling from 1.05 +/- 0.02 for targets alone to 0.98 +/- 0.01 (paired t test, p < 0.001).

fig3e-v4-fano-all-spacings: In V4, distractors at all spacings significantly reduce variability, the Fano factor falling from 1.00 +/- 0.01 for targets alone to 0.93 +/- 0.01 with the closest distractors (paired t test, p < 0.001 for each spacing).

Per neuron, the geometric mean over the four stimulus conditions of variance over mean; across neurons the geometric mean, with the SEM of the logs transformed back (exp(mean +/- SEM) given as a half-width). Conditions with zero mean or zero variance are left out (a standard choice); the paired t test is run on the Fano factors and on their logs.

FF = {}
rows = []
for area in AREAS:
    FF[(area, None)] = np.concatenate([cw.fano(p, "alone") for p in pops(area)])
    for s in SP:
        FF[(area, s)] = np.concatenate([cw.fano(p, "crowd", s) for p in pops(area)])
    a0 = FF[(area, None)]
    for s in [None] + list(SP):
        x = FF[(area, s)]
        lx = np.log(x[np.isfinite(x)])
        gm, sem = np.exp(lx.mean()), lx.std(ddof=1) / np.sqrt(len(lx))
        r = dict(area=area, condition="target alone" if s is None else SPL[s], n=int(np.isfinite(x).sum()),
                 geo_mean=gm, sem_halfwidth=gm * (np.exp(sem) - np.exp(-sem)) / 2)
        if s is not None:
            ok = np.isfinite(a0) & np.isfinite(x)
            t1 = stats.ttest_rel(a0[ok], x[ok])
            t2 = stats.ttest_rel(np.log(a0[ok]), np.log(x[ok]))
            r.update(t_ff=t1.statistic, p_ff=t1.pvalue, t_log=t2.statistic, p_log=t2.pvalue)
        rows.append(r)
ff = pd.DataFrame(rows)
print(ff.to_string(float_format=lambda v: f"{v:.4g}"))

Modulation indices (Figure 4)¶

fig4a-v1-modulation-indices: In V1, distractors at the closest spacing suppress and facilitate responses in roughly equal proportion, with significant suppression in 23% and facilitation in 27% of neurons; for farther distractors modulation is weaker, with 2.5% significant facilitation and 13% suppression.

fig4b-v4-modulation-indices: For the closest distractors most V4 neurons are facilitated (mean index 1.11 +/- 0.38, t test, p < 0.001; significant facilitation in 51% and suppression in 14% of cases), and the average index is larger than in V1 (one-sided t test, p < 0.01); at larger spacing facilitation and suppression are roughly equal (0.97 +/- 0.48; 24% and 32% significant).

Index per neuron and spacing: geometric mean over the four target orientations of the crowded over the target-alone mean count. Null: target-alone and crowded responses combined, resampled with replacement in the experimental numbers, 1000 times (STAR Methods); combined within each orientation or over all orientations. Tail rules: (a) two-sided, 2.5% per tail; (b) one-sided, 5% per direction. Neurons with a zero target-alone or crowded mean at some orientation have no index and are dropped.

rng = np.random.default_rng(4)
MI, NULL = {}, {}
for area in AREAS:
    for s in SP:
        MI[(area, s)] = np.concatenate([cw.modulation(p, s) for p in pops(area)])
        for pool in ("orientation", "all"):
            NULL[(area, s, pool)] = np.concatenate([cw.modulation_null(p, s, rng, pool=pool) for p in pops(area)])


def sig_counts(area, s, pool, rule):
    mi, nl = MI[(area, s)], NULL[(area, s, pool)]
    ok = np.isfinite(mi)
    # rank among the null draws that are defined (a draw is undefined when a resampled mean is 0)
    rank = np.sum(nl < mi[:, None], 1) / np.maximum(np.sum(np.isfinite(nl), 1), 1)
    tail = 0.025 if rule == "two-sided" else 0.05
    fac = ok & (rank > 1 - tail)
    sup = ok & (rank < tail)
    return ok, fac, sup


rows = []
for area in AREAS:
    for s in SP:
        for pool in ("orientation", "all"):
            for rule in ("two-sided", "one-sided"):
                ok, fac, sup = sig_counts(area, s, pool, rule)
                mi = MI[(area, s)][ok]
                rows.append(dict(area=area, spacing=SPL[s], pool=pool, rule=rule, n=int(ok.sum()),
                                 dropped=int((~ok).sum()), frac_above_1=np.mean(mi > 1), frac_below_1=np.mean(mi < 1),
                                 sig_fac_pct_all=100 * fac.sum() / ok.sum(), sig_sup_pct_all=100 * sup.sum() / ok.sum(),
                                 sig_fac_pct_of_facilitated=100 * fac.sum() / (mi > 1).sum(),
                                 sig_sup_pct_of_suppressed=100 * sup.sum() / (mi < 1).sum()))
        # farther spacings pooled (reading b)
for area in AREAS:
    for pool in ("orientation", "all"):
        for rule in ("two-sided", "one-sided"):
            oks, facs, sups, mis = [], [], [], []
            for s in SP[1:]:
                ok, fac, sup = sig_counts(area, s, pool, rule)
                oks.append(ok); facs.append(fac); sups.append(sup); mis.append(MI[(area, s)])
            ok, fac, sup, mi = map(np.concatenate, (oks, facs, sups, mis))
            mi = mi[ok]
            rows.append(dict(area=area, spacing="1.6-2.6 pooled", pool=pool, rule=rule, n=int(ok.sum()),
                             dropped=int((~ok).sum()), frac_above_1=np.mean(mi > 1), frac_below_1=np.mean(mi < 1),
                             sig_fac_pct_all=100 * fac.sum() / ok.sum(), sig_sup_pct_all=100 * sup.sum() / ok.sum(),
                             sig_fac_pct_of_facilitated=100 * fac.sum() / (mi > 1).sum(),
                             sig_sup_pct_of_suppressed=100 * sup.sum() / (mi < 1).sum()))

Result: fig4a-v1-modulation-indices partially reproduced. At 1.3 degrees, with the two-sided rule, 24.5% of V1 neurons are significantly suppressed and 26.5% facilitated (pooling within orientation; 24.7% and 26.0% pooling over all), within 23 +/- 2.3% and 27 +/- 2.7%; 56.6% have an index below 1 and 43.4% above. At farther spacings no reading puts both values within tolerance: at 2.6 degrees, two-sided, facilitation is 2.0% or 1.8% (expected 2.5 +/- 0.25) with suppression 14.4% or 12.9% (13 +/- 1.3); one-sided, facilitation is 2.5% or 2.3% but suppression 19.7% or 20.2%; pooled over the three farther spacings facilitation is 4.0 to 5.1%. The modulation is weaker at farther spacings, as the claim says, and the far percentages are near the paper's. At 2.6 degrees, two-sided and pooled within orientation, 2.0% is 8 of 396 neurons and 14.4% is 57; the tolerances (2.25 to 2.75% and 11.7 to 14.3%) correspond to 9 or 10 and 47 to 56 neurons, so each far value misses by one neuron. The facilitation tolerance of 0.25 points is about one neuron of 396, finer than the counts can resolve; this is asked of a reader in questions/henry-2022.yaml, and the claim is judged as the claims file has it.

Result: fig4b-v4-modulation-indices reproduced, under the two-sided rule with percentages of all neurons, the farthest spacing as "larger spacing", and the t tests on log indices. The V4 mean index at 1.3 degrees is 1.134 (SD 0.379, printed in the paper as +/- 0.38), with 69.8% of neurons above 1 and p = 1.9e-19 against 1; 50.7% are significantly facilitated and 15.1% (or 14.3%) suppressed. At 2.6 degrees the mean is 1.009 (SD 0.473), with 23.9% (23.5%) facilitated and 33.8% suppressed. All six values are within tolerance under both poolings. V4 against V1 at 1.3 degrees, one-sided: p = 0.009 on log indices, below 0.01, but p = 0.074 on the indices themselves (V1 mean 1.097), so this part rests on the log reading. With percentages of the facilitated and suppressed neurons as denominators, the values are far out (72.6% and 49.8%).

Modulation strength (Figure 4C)¶

fig4c-modulation-strength-significant: The strength of modulation, the mean absolute log modulation index, is significant in both areas at all spacings (permutation test, p < 0.01).

fig4c-v4-stronger-than-v1: Modulation strength is stronger in V4 than in V1 at all separations (one-sided t test, p = 0.01 for the closest distractors, p < 0.001 for the others).

fig4c-v4-maintained-v1-weaker-far: Modulation strength in V4 is largely maintained across spacings (one-sided t test nearest against farthest, p = 0.44), whereas in V1 the farthest separation yields weaker modulation than the nearest (one-sided t test, p < 0.001).

Strength per neuron is |log2 index|. The null is the per-neuron resampled indices above (both poolings), averaged over neurons in each of the 1000 resamples.

Tuning model (Figure 5, Figure S5, fit quality)¶

fig5bc-tuning-model-terms: With both terms allowed, V1 tuning amid distractors has a multiplicative term below 1 (0.59 +/- 0.03) and a positive additive term (0.39 +/- 0.16); in V4 the multiplicative term is 0.36 +/- 0.01 and the additive term 0.90 +/- 0.02; the multiplicative term is smaller and the additive term larger in V4 than in V1 (t test).

Neurons whose target-alone tuning from even and from odd presentations of each orientation (in stored order) correlates above 0.5. In V4 the stored order is not the recording order (data check), so there the split is in effect a random half split. Per neuron and spacing, rTD = max(mrT + amean(rT), 0), m and a by maximum Poisson likelihood, on single-trial counts (reading 1a) and on mean counts per orientation (1b).

In [17]:
REL = {area: np.concatenate([cw.even_odd_reliability(p) for p in pops(area)]) for area in AREAS}
for area in AREAS:
    print(f"{area}: reliability > 0.5 in {np.sum(REL[area] > 0.5)} of {len(REL[area])} neurons "
          f"(undefined in {np.sum(~np.isfinite(REL[area]))}); per animal "
          f"{ {an: int(np.sum((REL[area] > 0.5) & (animal[area] == an))) for an in ('AL', 'CA')} }")
# The V4 stored order is not the recording order (data check). Two order-free variants: the count
# passing under single random half splits (what an even/odd split of a random order gives), and
# REL_R, the reliability averaged over 20 random half splits, whose selection is fitted below too.
rng_sp = np.random.default_rng(13)
for area in AREAS:
    cnt = [sum(int(np.sum(cw.random_split_reliability(p, rng_sp, 1) > 0.5)) for p in pops(area)) for _ in range(20)]
    print(f"{area}: neurons above 0.5 under 20 single random half splits: mean {np.mean(cnt):.1f}, range {min(cnt)} to {max(cnt)}")
rng = np.random.default_rng(6)
REL_R = {area: np.concatenate([cw.random_split_reliability(p, rng) for p in pops(area)]) for area in AREAS}
for area in AREAS:
    print(f"{area}: REL_R (mean over 20 random splits) > 0.5 in {np.sum(REL_R[area] > 0.5)} neurons; per animal "
          f"{ {an: int(np.sum((REL_R[area] > 0.5) & (animal[area] == an))) for an in ('AL', 'CA')} }; "
          f"both selections {np.sum((REL[area] > 0.5) & (REL_R[area] > 0.5))}")


def fit_population(p, rel, single_trial):
    rows = []
    rT_all = cw.tuning(p, "alone")
    for i in np.flatnonzero(rel > 0.5):
        rT = rT_all[i]
        for s in SP:
            rc = [r[i] for r in cw.responses(p, "crowd", s)]
            m, a, ll = cw.fit_affine(rT, rc, single_trial)
            pred = np.maximum(m * rT + a * rT.mean(), cw.EPS)
            ll_null = cw._poisson_ll(np.full(len(rT), np.mean(np.concatenate(rc))), rc, True)
            ll_orac = cw._poisson_ll(np.array([c.mean() for c in rc]), rc, True)
            ll_mod = cw._poisson_ll(pred, rc, True)
            cm, llm = cw.fit_single(rT, rc, "mult", single_trial)
            ca, lla = cw.fit_single(rT, rc, "add", single_trial)
            rows.append(dict(area=p["area"], animal=p["animal"], session=p["session"], orange=p["orange"],
                             neuron=i, spacing=s, m=m, a=a, ll_null=ll_null, ll_oracle=ll_orac, ll_model=ll_mod,
                             c_mult=cm, c_add=ca, ll_mult=llm, ll_add=lla,
                             n_trials=[len(c) for c in rc]))
    return rows


t0 = time.time()
FIT = {}
for st in (True, False):
    res = Parallel(n_jobs=4)(delayed(fit_population)(p, cw.even_odd_reliability(p), st) for p in S)
    FIT[st] = pd.DataFrame([r for rr in res for r in rr])
offsets = {area: np.cumsum([0] + [p["counts"].shape[0] for p in pops(area)]) for area in AREAS}
rel_r_pop = [REL_R[p["area"]][offsets[p["area"]][k]:offsets[p["area"]][k + 1]]
             for area in AREAS for k, p in enumerate(pops(area))]
pop_order = [p for area in AREAS for p in pops(area)]
FIT_R = pd.DataFrame([r for rr in Parallel(n_jobs=4)(delayed(fit_population)(p, rl, True)
                                                     for p, rl in zip(pop_order, rel_r_pop)) for r in rr])
print(f"fits done in {time.time() - t0:.0f} s; cases per area:", FIT[True].groupby("area").size().to_dict(),
      "; random-split selection (REL_R):", FIT_R.groupby("area").size().to_dict())

rows = []
for st in (True, False):
    f = FIT[st]
    for unit in ("cases", "neurons"):
        g = f if unit == "cases" else f.groupby(["area", "session", "orange", "neuron"], as_index=False)[["m", "a"]].mean()
        r = dict(likelihood="single trial" if st else "means", unit=unit)
        for area in AREAS:
            x = g[g.area == area]
            r[f"{area}_n"] = len(x)
            r[f"{area}_m"] = x.m.mean(); r[f"{area}_m_sem"] = x.m.std(ddof=1) / np.sqrt(len(x))
            r[f"{area}_a"] = x.a.mean(); r[f"{area}_a_sem"] = x.a.std(ddof=1) / np.sqrt(len(x))
            r[f"{area}_m_below1_p"] = stats.ttest_1samp(x.m, 1, alternative="less").pvalue
        a1, a4 = g[g.area == "V1"], g[g.area == "V4"]
        r["m_V4_lt_V1_p_two_sided"] = stats.ttest_ind(a4.m, a1.m).pvalue
        r["m_V4_minus_V1"] = a4.m.mean() - a1.m.mean()
        r["a_V4_gt_V1_p_two_sided"] = stats.ttest_ind(a4.a, a1.a).pvalue
        r["a_V4_minus_V1"] = a4.a.mean() - a1.a.mean()
        rows.append(r)

Result: partially reproduced. The even/odd criterion keeps 146 V1 neurons, exactly the paper's count (89 and 57 per animal, as in Figure S7), and 244 V4 neurons against 198 +/- 20 (114 and 130 against 93 and 105). The V4 epochs are not stored in recording order (data check), but the order does not explain the excess: single random half splits keep 238.3 V4 neurons on average (219 to 256 over 20 splits) and 143.8 V1 neurons (126 to 163), so both stored-order counts lie in the range of random splits. The directions hold: m is below 1 in both areas (p < 1e-35), V4 has the smaller m (difference -0.251, p = 3.6e-18) and the larger a (+0.312, p = 3.7e-18). The values do not: over cases V1 m = 0.405 +/- 0.023 and a = 0.596 +/- 0.026 (expected 0.59 and 0.39), V4 m = 0.154 +/- 0.017 (expected 0.36) and a = 0.907 +/- 0.023, the only one within tolerance. Fits on means and averages over neurons change these by less than 0.001. On the selection by reliability averaged over 20 random splits (109 V1 and 160 V4 neurons, below) the picture is the same: m 0.403 and 0.178, a 0.588 and 0.894, only the V4 additive term within tolerance, and the V4 differences at p = 4.1e-16 and 1.9e-14.

fit-quality¶

In the neurons fitted with the tuning model, the fit quality (a normalized likelihood between a null model at 0 and an oracle at 1) is 0.63 in V1 and 0.73 in V4.

fig5-terms-covary¶

In both V1 and V4 the additive and multiplicative terms covary strongly, consistent with a flattening of tuning with maintained responsivity.

Result: reproduced. m and a are strongly and negatively correlated: Pearson r = -0.892 in V1 (584 cases) and -0.682 in V4 (976 cases), p below 1e-130 (Spearman -0.955 and -0.839). Over 20 single random half splits, each keeping the neurons whose reliability on that split is above 0.5 (below), r is -0.966 to -0.854 in V1 and -0.893 to -0.639 in V4 (medians -0.886 and -0.683), so the criterion holds on all 20 and the stored-order split is typical of single splits. Only the selection by reliability averaged over 20 random splits, which keeps fewer neurons (160 in V4), gives V4 r = -0.459 (p = 1.1e-34), below the criterion's 0.5 (V1 -0.913). The outcome rests on a single split, as the paper's rule describes, and is marked as resting on that assumption.

Some fits give a negative multiplicative term, offset by a large additive term; such cases are rare in V1 and more frequent in V4.

Result: partially reproduced. Negative multiplicative terms are more frequent in V4 (35.1% of cases) than in V1 (23.3%; Fisher p = 7.7e-07), and they come with large additive terms (mean a 1.29 and 1.41 against 0.38 and 0.63). But 23.3% of V1 cases is not rare by the criterion's reading (below 10%). On the random-split selection (below) the fractions are 20.2% and 33.6% (Fisher p = 1.3e-06), the same partial outcome.

fig5de-simulated-discriminability¶

Simulating crowded responses with the fitted multiplicative and additive terms yields some loss of discriminability in V1 and more in V4, similar to but slightly stronger than the measured loss, and depending weakly on spacing.

For each fitted neuron and spacing, Poisson counts at the two extreme orientations with the measured target-alone means and with the model's prediction (single-trial fits); AUC with the preferred extreme as in Figure 2; OLS slope with 1000 bootstrap samples. Trials per stimulus: (a) as recorded, (b) 1000. Measured slopes: (a) Figure 2C over all neurons, (b) the fitted neurons only.

In [21]:
rng = np.random.default_rng(5)
popkey = {(p["area"], p["session"], p["orange"]): p for p in S}


def simulate_aucs(f, mode, rng, rule="affine"):
    """Simulated (alone, crowded) AUCs per case. rule 'affine' uses m and a; 'single' the
    additive fit when the case's index is above 1 and the multiplicative one otherwise."""
    out = []
    for _, r in f.iterrows():
        p = popkey[(r.area, r.session, r.orange)]
        first, second = cw.extreme_order(p)
        rT = cw.tuning(p, "alone")[r.neuron]
        if rule == "affine":
            pred = np.maximum(r.m * rT + r.a * rT.mean(), 0)
        elif r.mi > 1:
            pred = np.maximum(rT + r.c_add * rT.mean(), 0)
        else:
            pred = np.maximum(r.c_mult * rT, 0)
        ra, rc = cw.responses(p, "alone"), cw.responses(p, "crowd", r.spacing)
        if mode == "recorded":
            na1, na2, nc1, nc2 = ra[first].shape[1], ra[second].shape[1], rc[first].shape[1], rc[second].shape[1]
        else:
            na1 = na2 = nc1 = nc2 = 1000
        a = cw.auc(rng.poisson(rT[first], na1), rng.poisson(rT[second], na2))
        c = cw.auc(rng.poisson(pred[first], nc1), rng.poisson(pred[second], nc2))
        out.append((a, c))
    return np.array(out)

Result: reproduced. Under reading (a) of both open details (recorded trial counts, Figure 2C slopes over all neurons) the simulated V4 slope is below the V1 slope at every spacing (0.243 to 0.336 against 0.404 to 0.567), and the simulated slope is at or below the measured one at 4 of 4 spacings in V1 and 3 of 4 in V4 (V4 at 1.3 degrees: 0.243 against 0.206). The criterion is also met with recorded trial counts against the fitted neurons' own slopes (4 of 4 in each area) and with 1000 trials against the fitted neurons' slopes (V4 3 of 4); with 1000 trials against all neurons V4 is at or below the measured slope at only 1 of 4 spacings. Reading (a, a) is near its limit: over 20 single random splits (below) it holds on 11, and on the stored-order split with another simulation draw V4 is at or below at 2 of 4. Against the fitted neurons' own slopes with recorded trial counts the criterion holds on all 20 single random splits and on the selection by reliability averaged over 20 random splits (V4 4 of 4; below), where reading (a, a) gives V4 at or below at 1 of 4 spacings (2 of 4 with another draw). The outcome was marked as resting on the even/odd selection because reading (a, a) fails on the averaged selection; under the reading against the fitted neurons' slopes it holds on every selection tested.

figs5-additive-vs-multiplicative¶

Fitting either a multiplicative or an additive change of target tuning alone, neurons facilitated by distractors are better described by the additive model and suppressed neurons by the multiplicative model, in V1 and V4; each single form reduces discriminability, but less than in the measured responses.

Single-form fits on the same cases (the tuning model's neuron selection); log-likelihood ratio, multiplicative over additive, against the case's modulation index. Panels C and D: the simulation above with the additive fit for facilitated cases and the multiplicative fit for suppressed ones (rows model == single). The all-driven-neurons variant of the selection is shown below.

for st in (True, False):
    f = FIT[st].copy()
    f["mi"] = fitted["mi"].values
    f["llr"] = f.ll_mult - f.ll_add
    for area in AREAS:
        x = f[f.area == area]
        fac, sup = x[x.mi > 1], x[x.mi < 1]
        print(f"fits on {'single trials' if st else 'means'}: {area} facilitated cases favouring additive (LLR < 0): "
              f"{(fac.llr < 0).sum()} of {len(fac)} ({100 * (fac.llr < 0).mean():.1f}%); suppressed favouring "
              f"multiplicative (LLR > 0): {(sup.llr > 0).sum()} of {len(sup)} ({100 * (sup.llr > 0).mean():.1f}%)")


def single_form_all(p):
    rows = []
    rT_all = cw.tuning(p, "alone")
    for i in range(p["counts"].shape[0]):
        mi = {s: cw.modulation(p, s)[i] for s in SP}
        for s in SP:
            rc = [r[i] for r in cw.responses(p, "crowd", s)]
            _, llm = cw.fit_single(rT_all[i], rc, "mult")
            _, lla = cw.fit_single(rT_all[i], rc, "add")
            rows.append(dict(area=p["area"], mi=mi[s], llr=llm - lla))
    return rows


allf = pd.DataFrame([r for rr in Parallel(n_jobs=4)(delayed(single_form_all)(p) for p in S) for r in rr])
for area in AREAS:

    fac, sup = x[x.mi > 1], x[x.mi < 1]

Result: reproduced. Among the tuning model's cases, 89.8% of facilitated V1 cases and 97.0% of facilitated V4 cases favour the additive model, and 83.7% and 92.1% of suppressed cases favour the multiplicative one; over all neurons 86.1%, 92.2%, 81.0% and 88.5%. The single-form simulation (additive for facilitation, multiplicative for suppression) gives slopes below 1 at every spacing (point slopes 0.776 to 0.911 with recorded trial counts; judged by the upper CI instead, V1 at 2.6 degrees reaches 1.001), above the measured Figure 2 slopes at 4 of 4 spacings in each area. On the random-split selection (below) the shares are 93.1%, 98.0%, 84.9% and 93.2% and the single-form slopes 0.807 to 0.887, above the measured ones at 4 of 4 spacings in each area.

Tuning-model claims on the random-split selection¶

The fig5bc, fit-quality, fig5-terms-covary, fig5-negative-multiplicative, fig5de and figs5 tests repeated on the neurons selected by REL_R (reliability averaged over 20 random half splits, single-trial likelihood, means over cases), since the V4 stored order is not the recording order.

# fig5-terms-covary and fig5de over 20 single random half splits. The even/odd split in stored order
# is one half split; this shows whether its V4 r and fig5de comparison are typical of single random
# splits. Every neuron is fitted once (single-trial likelihood), and each split selects the neurons
# whose reliability on that split is above 0.5.
def fit_all(p):
    rT_all = cw.tuning(p, "alone")
    rows = []
    for s in SP:
        rc_all = cw.responses(p, "crowd", s)
        for i in range(p["counts"].shape[0]):
            m, a, _ = cw.fit_affine(rT_all[i], [r[i] for r in rc_all], True)
            rows.append(dict(area=p["area"], session=p["session"], orange=p["orange"], neuron=i, spacing=s, m=m, a=a))
    return rows


t0 = time.time()
ALLFIT = pd.DataFrame([r for rr in Parallel(n_jobs=4)(delayed(fit_all)(p) for p in S) for r in rr])
ALLFIT = ALLFIT.sort_values(["area", "session", "orange", "neuron", "spacing"], kind="stable").reset_index(drop=True)
chk = FIT[True].merge(ALLFIT, on=["area", "session", "orange", "neuron", "spacing"], suffixes=("", "_all"))
print(f"all {len(ALLFIT)} neuron and spacing cases fitted in {time.time() - t0:.0f} s; largest difference from the "
      f"even/odd fits: m {np.abs(chk.m - chk.m_all).max():.2g}, a {np.abs(chk.a - chk.a_all).max():.2g} ({len(chk)} cases)")
key_order = ALLFIT.drop_duplicates(["area", "session", "orange"])[["area", "session", "orange"]].itertuples(index=False)
pops_sorted = [popkey[tuple(k)] for k in key_order]
AUC_A = {id(p): cw.neuron_aucs(p, "alone") for p in S}
AUC_C = {(id(p), s): cw.neuron_aucs(p, "crowd", s) for p in S for s in SP}


def split_tests(selected, rng):
    """Pearson r of m and a per area, and the fig5de comparison under the four readings."""
    x = ALLFIT[selected]
    out = {}
    for area in AREAS:
        xa = x[x.area == area]
        out[f"{area}_neurons"] = len(xa) // 4
        out[f"{area}_r"] = stats.pearsonr(xa.m, xa.a)[0]
    sl = {}
    for mode in ("recorded", "1000"):
        for area in AREAS:
            for s in SP:
                xs = x[(x.area == area) & (x.spacing == s)]
                ac = simulate_aucs(xs, mode, rng)
                sl[(mode, area, s)] = cw.ols_slope(ac[:, 0], ac[:, 1])
    meas_f = {}
    for area in AREAS:
        for s in SP:
            xs = x[(x.area == area) & (x.spacing == s)]
            pp = [popkey[(r.area, r.session, r.orange)] for r in xs.itertuples()]
            meas_f[(area, s)] = cw.ols_slope([AUC_A[id(p)][r.neuron] for p, r in zip(pp, xs.itertuples())],
                                             [AUC_C[(id(p), s)][r.neuron] for p, r in zip(pp, xs.itertuples())])
    for mode in ("recorded", "1000"):
        below = all(sl[(mode, "V4", s)] < sl[(mode, "V1", s)] for s in SP)
        out[f"{mode}_V4_below_V1"] = below
        for meas in ("all", "fitted"):
            for area in AREAS:
                ref = {s: (f2[(f2.area == area) & (f2.spacing == SPL[s])].iloc[0].slope if meas == "all"
                           else meas_f[(area, s)]) for s in SP}
                out[f"{mode}_{meas}_{area}"] = sum(sl[(mode, area, s)] <= ref[s] for s in SP)
            out[f"{mode}_{meas}_pass"] = below and out[f"{mode}_{meas}_V1"] >= 3 and out[f"{mode}_{meas}_V4"] >= 3
    return out


t0 = time.time()
rng_split, rng_sim = np.random.default_rng(16), np.random.default_rng(17)
rows = []
for k in range(21):
    if k == 0:   # the even/odd split in stored order, the main selection
        rel = [cw.even_odd_reliability(p) for p in pops_sorted]
    else:
        rel = [cw.random_split_reliability(p, rng_split, 1) for p in pops_sorted]
    selected = np.concatenate([np.repeat(r > 0.5, len(SP)) for r in rel])
    rows.append(dict(split="even/odd" if k == 0 else f"random {k}", **split_tests(selected, rng_sim)))
SPLITS = pd.DataFrame(rows)
print(f"21 selections in {time.time() - t0:.0f} s")

The first row is the even/odd split in stored order, the main selection; its fits are the same as the main fits (largest difference 0). Single random half splits keep 137 to 162 V1 and 216 to 271 V4 neurons. Over the 20 of them V4 r is -0.893 to -0.639 and V1 r -0.966 to -0.854, so fig5-terms-covary holds on every one; the stored-order V4 r (-0.682) is at their median (-0.683). For fig5de, with recorded trial counts, the V4 simulated slope is at or below the measured slope of the selected neurons at 3 or 4 of 4 spacings on every split (criterion met on 20 of 20), and at or below the Figure 2C slope over all neurons at 2 of 4 on 9 splits, 3 of 4 on 10 and 4 of 4 on 1 (met on 11 of 20). With 1000 trials the criterion is met on 19 of 20 against the selected neurons and on none against all neurons. The simulation is redrawn here, so the stored-order row can differ from the fig5de cell (V4 2 of 4 against all neurons here, 3 of 4 there).

Tuning correlations (Figure 6C to 6E)¶

fig6c-tuning-correlation-near: Tuning for targets alone correlates well with tuning for targets with nearby distractors in V1 (0.38 +/- 0.03 for cells above a reliability criterion of 0.5), and significantly less in V4 (0.22 +/- 0.03; one-sided t test, p < 0.001).

fig6d-tuning-correlation-spacing: Target tuning with near and with far distractors correlates less in V4 than V1 (0.17 +/- 0.02 against 0.36 +/- 0.02 at criterion 0.5; one-sided t test, p < 0.001).

fig6e-tuning-correlation-configuration: In 4 further sessions, target tuning with two distractor configurations whose orientations differ by 20 degrees differs substantially in V4 (correlation 0.24 +/- 0.06) and is nearly unaffected in V1 (0.65 +/- 0.06; p < 0.001, one-sided t test).

Reliability as for the tuning model (even and odd presentations in stored order); Pearson correlation of mean count per target orientation between two conditions; mean +/- SEM over neurons; V1 greater than V4 by a one-sided two-sample t test (Student, Welch shown too).

In [25]:
def tuning_pooled(p, seps):
    """Mean count per orientation over the epochs of several spacings."""
    return np.stack([np.concatenate([cw.responses(p, "crowd", s)[o] for s in seps], 1).mean(1)
                     for o in range(len(p["oris"]))], 1)


TC = {}
for area in AREAS:
    ta = np.concatenate([cw.tuning(p, "alone") for p in pops(area)])
    near_a = np.concatenate([cw.tuning(p, "crowd", 1.32) for p in pops(area)])
    near_b = np.concatenate([tuning_pooled(p, SP[:2]) for p in pops(area)])
    far_a = np.concatenate([cw.tuning(p, "crowd", 2.56) for p in pops(area)])
    far_b = np.concatenate([tuning_pooled(p, SP[2:]) for p in pops(area)])
    TC[(area, "6C (a) alone vs 1.3")] = cw.rowcorr(ta, near_a)
    TC[(area, "6C (b) alone vs 1.3+1.6")] = cw.rowcorr(ta, near_b)
    TC[(area, "6D (a) 1.3 vs 2.6")] = cw.rowcorr(near_a, far_a)
    TC[(area, "6D (b) 1.3+1.6 vs 2.1+2.6")] = cw.rowcorr(near_b, far_b)


def compare(key, crit, rel):
    out = {}
    for area in AREAS:
        x = TC[(area, key)][(rel[area] > crit)]
        out[area] = x[np.isfinite(x)]
    t = ttest_1s_greater(out["V1"], out["V4"])
    tw = ttest_1s_greater(out["V1"], out["V4"], False)
    return out, t.pvalue, tw.pvalue

for key in ["6C (a) alone vs 1.3", "6C (b) alone vs 1.3+1.6", "6D (a) 1.3 vs 2.6", "6D (b) 1.3+1.6 vs 2.1+2.6"]:
    for crit in (0.5, 0.7, 0.9):
        out, p_, pw = compare(key, crit, REL)
        rows.append(dict(comparison=key, criterion=crit, V1_n=len(out["V1"]), V1_mean=out["V1"].mean(),

A random half split gives a reliability that does not depend on the stored order. As the V4 order is not the recording order, the comparison is repeated with reliability from 20 random half splits of each orientation's presentations (mean correlation over splits), as a variant (REL_R, computed in the fig5bc section).

At criterion 0.5, reading (a), V1 gives 0.389 +/- 0.042, within 0.38 +/- 0.03, and V4 0.161 +/- 0.039, below 0.22 +/- 0.03; reading (b) gives 0.460 (out) and 0.238 (within). V4 is lower than V1 at p = 8.9e-05 (a) and 1.2e-04 (b), and at criteria 0.7 and 0.9 too (p = 5.9e-05 and 0.009). No reading puts both values within tolerance; the V4 value is lower than the paper's, a larger effect.

Result: fig6d-tuning-correlation-spacing partially reproduced. Near against far tuning correlates less in V4 than V1 (reading a: 0.135 against 0.432, p = 1.2e-06; reading b: 0.214 against 0.515, p = 1.8e-07), but no value is within tolerance of 0.17 +/- 0.02 and 0.36 +/- 0.02. The random-split variant of the reliability gives the same picture (V1 0.374 against V4 0.132).

Result: reproduced. In the orientation experiment, at criterion 0.5, the tuning with the two distractor configurations correlates 0.644 +/- 0.061 in V1 (50 neurons) and 0.214 +/- 0.047 in V4 (90 neurons), within 0.65 +/- 0.06 and 0.24 +/- 0.06; V1 exceeds V4 at p = 6.7e-08. The same holds at criteria 0.7 and 0.9 (p = 2.1e-05 and 0.006).

figs6-common-neuron-pool¶

The distinct V4 decoding axes for different displays do not arise from relying on distinct subsets of neurons; most target-responsive neurons remain driven with distractors, and the most informative neuron for targets alone remains informative with distractors.

Driven: mean count above the blank mean plus 1 SD of the blank counts (Figure S6 legend), to targets alone and, for those, to targets with distractors at each spacing. Informativeness: |d'| between the two extreme targets, normalized by the population's summed |d'| in that condition.

In [28]:
rows = []
for p in S:
    bl = p["counts"][:, cw.stim_mask(p, "blank")]
    thr = bl.mean(1) + bl.std(1, ddof=1)
    drv = p["counts"][:, cw.stim_mask(p, "alone")].mean(1) > thr
    r = dict(area=p["area"], session=p["session"], orange=p["orange"], n=len(thr), driven=drv.mean())
    for s in SP:
        dc = p["counts"][:, cw.stim_mask(p, "crowd", s)].mean(1) > thr
        r[f"still_{SPL[s]}"] = dc[drv].mean() if drv.any() else np.nan
    first, second = cw.extreme_order(p)
    dps = {}
    for cond, s in (("alone", None), ("near", 1.32), ("far", 2.56)):
        rr = cw.responses(p, "alone" if s is None else "crowd", s)
        d = np.abs(np.array([cw.dprime(rr[first][i], rr[second][i]) for i in range(len(thr))]))
        d[~np.isfinite(d)] = 0
        dps[cond] = d / d.sum()
    top = int(np.argmax(dps["alone"]))
    r.update(top_alone=dps["alone"][top], top_near=dps["near"][top], top_far=dps["far"][top])
    rows.append(r)

Result: reproduced. The driven fractions cover only the 10 of 22 populations per area (sessions 3 to 7) in which at least one unit's target-alone mean exceeds its blank mean by 1 SD. In the other 12 no unit passes this threshold, although 8% to 86% of V1 units and 23% to 75% of V4 units there have a target-alone mean above their blank mean (data check). In those 10, the mean fraction of target-driven units still driven with distractors is 0.944 to 0.960 in V1 and 0.866 to 0.953 in V4, at least 0.8 at every spacing. The top-unit test covers all 22 populations: the most informative unit for targets alone keeps its share of the population's d' with distractors, across V4 populations r = 0.672 (p = 0.0006) with near and 0.803 (p = 6.8e-06) with far distractors (V1: 0.855 and 0.921). The fraction driven by targets alone is 0.817 (V1) and 0.871 (V4) over the 10 populations, above the range of Figure S6A (0.3 to 0.5); its means over all 22 populations (0.372 and 0.396) fall in that range only because the 12 populations with no driven unit count as 0. The criterion does not test this fraction.

Population decoding¶

One L1 logistic decoder per population, pair of target orientations (six pairs) and condition (targets alone, or with distractors at each spacing), fitted and tested by cross-validation as the STAR Methods describe. Runs: main (10 outer and 10 inner folds), folds5 (5 and 5, the variant), shuffled_all (each neuron's counts shuffled across trials of the same stimulus before decoding, reading (a) of fig3c) and shuffled_train (training trials shuffled, test trials intact, reading (b)). Each population's run has its own seeded generator. Timed on two populations first: about 1 s per decoder for main.

In [29]:
PAIRS = [(0, 1), (1, 2), (2, 3), (0, 2), (1, 3), (0, 3)]
CONDS = [("alone", None)] + [("crowd", s) for s in SP]
MODES = {"main": (10, 10), "folds5": (5, 5), "shuffled_all": (10, 10), "shuffled_train": (10, 10)}


def decode_population(pi, mode):
    p = S[pi]
    outer, inner = MODES[mode]
    rng = np.random.default_rng([7, pi, list(MODES).index(mode)])
    rows = []
    for a, b in PAIRS:
        for kind, s in CONDS:
            X, y = cw.pair_trials(p, kind, s, a, b)
            diag = []
            if mode == "shuffled_all":
                perf = cw.decode(cw.shuffle_within(X, y, rng), y, rng, outer, inner, diag)
            elif mode == "shuffled_train":
                perf = cw.decode_shuffled_train(X, y, rng, outer, inner)
            else:
                perf = cw.decode(X, y, rng, outer, inner, diag)
            rows.append(dict(mode=mode, area=p["area"], animal=p["animal"], session=p["session"], orange=p["orange"],
                             a=a, b=b, sep_deg=6 * (b - a), cond="alone" if s is None else s, perf=perf, n=len(y),
                             n_test=len(y) / outer, Cs=[c for c, _, _ in diag], nonzero=[k for _, k, _ in diag],
                             perf_nonzero=float(np.mean([v for _, _, v in diag])) if diag else np.nan))
    return rows


t0 = time.time()
DEC = []
for mode in MODES:
    t1 = time.time()
    res = Parallel(n_jobs=4)(delayed(decode_population)(pi, mode) for pi in range(len(S)))
    DEC += [r for rr in res for r in rr]
    print(f"{mode}: {len(S) * len(PAIRS) * len(CONDS)} decoders in {time.time() - t1:.0f} s")
DEC = pd.DataFrame(DEC)
print(f"decoding total {time.time() - t0:.0f} s; peak memory {resource.getrusage(resource.RUSAGE_SELF).ru_maxrss / 1e6:.2f} GB")
print(DEC.groupby(["mode", "area", "cond"]).perf.agg(["count", "mean", "min", "max"]).round(3).to_string())


def paired_points(mode, area, s, animal_=None):
    d = DEC[(DEC["mode"] == mode) & (DEC.area == area)]
    if animal_ is not None:
        d = d[d.animal == animal_]
    al = d[d.cond == "alone"].set_index(["session", "orange", "a", "b"])
    cr = d[d.cond == s].set_index(["session", "orange", "a", "b"])
    j = al.add_suffix("_alone").join(cr.add_suffix("_crowd"))
    return j.reset_index()

# penalty leaves no nonzero coefficient (the decoder then predicts one class for every test trial).
dm = DEC[DEC["mode"] == "main"]
rows = []
for (area, cond), d in dm.groupby(["area", "cond"]):
    cs = np.concatenate(d.Cs.values)
    nz = np.concatenate(d.nonzero.values)
    r = dict(area=area, cond=cond, folds=len(cs), frac_all_zero=np.mean(nz == 0), median_nonzero=np.median(nz))
    for c in cw.CS:
        r[f"C={c:.2g}"] = np.mean(np.isclose(cs, c))

In 9.9% to 14.5% of the main run's outer folds in V1, and 4.8% (targets alone) to 18.4% (1.3 degrees) in V4, the chosen penalty is the largest of the grid (C = 0.01) and leaves no nonzero coefficient, so the decoder predicts one class for every held-out trial of the fold. The paper's rule (the largest penalty that reaches the maximal cross-validated performance) selects such a decoder whenever no smaller penalty does better on the inner folds; how often it does depends on the grid's lower bound, a choice made here. In the variant, each such decoder is replaced by the one at the smallest larger C that has a nonzero coefficient, on the same folds. Mean performances change by at most 0.007 (V1 targets alone 0.584 to 0.591, V1 at 2.6 degrees 0.576 to 0.583), so the all-zero decoders do not pull the performances to chance on average.

fig2de-population-decoding-example¶

In one animal at the nearest spacing, V4 population decoding performance with distractors tends to be lower than for targets alone when performance is above chance (p < 0.001), while in V1 the loss is not significant (p > 0.05).

The animal with 84 cases (6 pairs x 14 populations) is AL; CA has 48. Both are shown.

Result: reproduced, with V1 taken over all cases. In AL at 1.3 degrees (84 cases), V4 performance with distractors is lower where target-alone performance exceeds 0.5 (74 cases, 0.645 against 0.536, paired t p = 1.5e-15, Wilcoxon p = 2.8e-11). In V1 the difference over all 84 cases is not significant (0.560 against 0.552, p = 0.46 and 0.60), but restricted as V4 is it is (62 cases, p = 0.018 and 0.025), so the V1 part rests on the unrestricted reading. The 5-fold variant and the other animal give the same pattern.

Threshold elevation (Figure 2F)¶

fig2f-v1-threshold-elevation: In V1, distractors elevate the estimated discrimination threshold of the populations by 1.31 +/- 0.10 at the closest spacing and 1.15 +/- 0.08 at the farthest, significant at all but the farthest spacing (permutation test, p < 0.05).

fig2f-v4-threshold-elevation: In V4 the estimated threshold elevations are greater than in V1, 2.52 +/- 0.23 for the closest distractors and 1.89 +/- 0.19 for the farthest, significant at all spacings (permutation test, p < 0.001).

Per animal, area and spacing, k by maximum likelihood over the (target alone, crowded) points of all pairs and populations; points with target-alone performance at or below 0.5 or at 1 dropped. Binomial trial count: (a) the held-out trials of one fold, (b) all trials of the pair; since the held-out count is a tenth of the total for every point, the two scale the likelihood by a constant and give the same k, so they differ only in the bootstrap and permutation draws. The Figure 2F value is the mean of the two animals' estimates; its SEM is the SD of that mean over 1000 bootstrap samples of each animal's points; the permutation test swaps the two labels at random within each point, 1000 times, refits both animals and averages; the table gives the median and the 5th and 95th percentiles of that null. The k grid runs from 0.2 to 20; k_wide repeats the estimate on a grid up to 1000 to show where the bound censors it.

In [32]:
def elevation(mode, area, s, ntrials, rng, n_boot=1000, n_perm=1000):
    ests, boots, perms, used, wide = [], [], [], [], []
    for an in ("AL", "CA"):
        j = paired_points(mode, area, s, an)
        n = j.n_test_crowd.values if ntrials == "fold" else j.n_crowd.values
        pa, pc = j.perf_alone.values, j.perf_crowd.values
        ests.append(cw.fit_k(pa, pc, n))
        wide.append(cw.fit_k(pa, pc, n, cw.K_GRID_WIDE))
        boots.append(cw.boot_k(pa, pc, n, rng, n_boot) if n_boot else None)
        perms.append(cw.perm_k(pa, pc, n, rng, n_perm) if n_perm else None)
        used.append(f"{int(cw.usable(pa).sum())}/{len(pa)}")
    out = dict(mode=mode, area=area, spacing=SPL[s], ntrials=ntrials, k_AL=ests[0], k_CA=ests[1], k=np.mean(ests),
               points_used=" ".join(used), k_AL_wide=wide[0], k_CA_wide=wide[1], k_wide=np.mean(wide))
    if n_boot:
        out["sem"] = np.std((boots[0] + boots[1]) / 2, ddof=1)
    if n_perm:
        null = (perms[0] + perms[1]) / 2
        out["p_perm"] = (1 + np.sum(null >= out["k"])) / (1 + len(null))
        out["null_median"], out["null_5"], out["null_95"] = np.percentile(null, [50, 5, 95])
    return out

# Calibration of the threshold-elevation estimate: with no crowding (true k = 1), crowded and
# target-alone performances drawn as binomial fractions around each case's recorded target-alone
# performance, with the recorded trial count of the pair; k estimated as above, mean of the two
# animals, 200 simulations per area and spacing.
rng = np.random.default_rng(15)
rows = []
for area in AREAS:
    for s in SP:
        ks = []
        for _ in range(200):
            e = []
            for an in ("AL", "CA"):
                j = paired_points("main", area, s, an)
                n = j.n_crowd.values
                pt = np.clip(j.perf_alone.values, 0.5, 1)
                e.append(cw.fit_k(rng.binomial(n, pt) / n, rng.binomial(n, pt) / n, n))
            ks.append(np.mean(e))
        ks = np.array(ks)
        rows.append(dict(area=area, spacing=SPL[s], k_null_mean=ks.mean(), k_null_median=np.median(ks),
                         k_null_5=np.percentile(ks, 5), k_null_95=np.percentile(ks, 95)))
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).round(3).to_string())

With no crowding the estimate is biased upward: its mean is 1.17 to 1.18 in V1 (5th to 95th percentile 1.07 to 1.29) and 1.09 in V4 (1.02 to 1.16), because points near chance enter the fit by noise. The permutation nulls are shifted further: their medians are 1.37 to 1.63 in V1 and 1.75 to 4.16 in V4 (main run), well above the no-crowding calibration, so the permutation null is not calibrated by it. Judged against the calibration, every V1 estimate (1.50 to 1.69) would count as elevated; judged against the permutation null, only 2.1 degrees does. The V1 significance pattern therefore depends on the null and says little either way; the V1 outcome rests on the values.

Result: not reproduced. The V1 threshold elevation is 1.685 +/- 0.351 at 1.3 degrees and 1.669 +/- 0.314 at 2.6, outside 1.31 +/- 0.10 and 1.15 +/- 0.08. The permutation test finds only 2.1 degrees significant (p = 0.048 and 0.047 for the two trial counts), not 1.3 or 1.6 (p = 0.18 to 0.42) and not 2.6 (p = 0.059 and 0.062); with 5 folds no spacing is significant. The two trial counts are one reading for the estimate (same k). The V1 estimates are above the no-crowding calibration (95th percentile 1.26 to 1.29) and near the medians of their permutation nulls (1.63 at 1.3 degrees, 1.49 at 2.6). The null is shifted much further than the calibration, so the significance pattern says little in either direction; the outcome rests on the values, which fail. Without all-zero decoders the values are 1.688 and 1.575, also outside.

Result: partially reproduced. V4 elevations exceed V1 at every spacing and the permutation test gives p = 0.001 (the smallest attainable) at all four spacings, but the values are far from the paper's: 7.30 +/- 2.47 at 1.3 degrees and 2.61 +/- 0.29 at 2.6, against 2.52 +/- 0.23 and 1.89 +/- 0.19. The CA estimates are large (10.87 and 18.52 at 1.3 and 1.6 degrees); on the grid up to 1000 they are 10.87 and 18.47, so the bound of 20 does not censor the main run (in the 5-fold run CA at 1.6 degrees reaches it, 41.0 on the wider grid). The AL estimates are 3.74 and 1.83 at the closest and farthest spacings. The V4 estimates are far above their permutation null medians (3.51 at 1.3 degrees, 1.75 at 2.6). Without all-zero decoders V4 gives 6.91 and 2.55, and CA 10.46 at 1.3 degrees, so these decoders do not explain the large CA estimates.

Result: reproduced. With shuffled responses the threshold elevations lie within twice the bootstrap SEM of the original estimates at 8 of 8 area and spacing pairs, and V4 exceeds V1 at every spacing, under both readings (shuffling all trials or only the training trials) and both trial counts. The comparison is with this attempt's own original estimates, which differ from the paper's (fig2f claims). The test is lenient where the SEMs are large (V4 2.0 to 2.5 at 1.3 to 2.1 degrees).

fig7cd-fixed-decoder-generalization¶

Projected onto the decoding axis of the opposite condition, discriminability is largely preserved in V1 (d' 0.95 +/- 0.13 same, 0.88 +/- 0.12 cross, p = 0.20) but drops significantly in V4 (1.02 +/- 0.13 against 0.67 +/- 0.05, p = 0.002, paired t test).

Per population, two L1 logistic decoders (penalty as above) on the two most different target orientations, one on targets alone and one with distractors at 1.3 degrees. Ten folds over all trials of both conditions and all four orientations; in each, both decoders are fitted on the training trials of the extremes and the held-out trials of all orientations, in both conditions, are projected onto both axes. d' = (mu2 - mu1) / sqrt(0.5 (s1^2 + s2^2)) per pair of orientations (signed so that the trained direction is positive). Readings: unit of the test (a) population, averaged over pairs and both conditions, or (b) population x pair x condition; pairs (all, or the 18 degree pair alone).

In [38]:
def fixed_axes(pi):
    p = S[pi]
    rng = np.random.default_rng([10, pi])
    m = cw.stim_mask(p, "alone") | cw.stim_mask(p, "crowd", 1.32)
    idx = np.flatnonzero(m)
    X = p["counts"][:, idx].T.astype(float)
    cond = (p["p"].kind.values[idx] == "crowd").astype(int)
    oi = p["p"].oi.values[idx]
    folds = cw._folds(cond * 10 + oi, 10, rng)
    proj = np.full((len(idx), 2, 2), np.nan)   # last axis: the decoder as chosen, and cw.fit_nonzero
    n_zero = 0
    for j in range(10):
        tr, te = folds != j, folds == j
        for axis in (0, 1):
            sel = tr & (cond == axis) & np.isin(oi, (0, 3))
            Xa, ya = X[sel], (oi[sel] == 3).astype(int)
            C = cw.choose_C(Xa, ya, 10, rng)
            Xtr, Xte = cw._zscore(Xa, X[te])
            coef, b = cw._fit(Xtr, ya, C)
            proj[te, axis, 0] = Xte @ coef + b
            if not np.any(coef != 0):
                n_zero += 1
                coef, b = cw.fit_nonzero(Xtr, ya, C)
            proj[te, axis, 1] = Xte @ coef + b
    rows = []
    for a, b_ in PAIRS:
        for c in (0, 1):
            for axis in (0, 1):
                x1 = proj[(cond == c) & (oi == a), axis]
                x2 = proj[(cond == c) & (oi == b_), axis]
                rows.append(dict(area=p["area"], animal=p["animal"], session=p["session"], orange=p["orange"], a=a, b=b_,
                                 sep_deg=6 * (b_ - a), data="alone" if c == 0 else "crowded",
                                 axis="alone" if axis == 0 else "crowded", same=c == axis, dprime=cw.dprime(x2[:, 0], x1[:, 0]),
                                 dprime_nonzero=cw.dprime(x2[:, 1], x1[:, 1]), zero_fits=n_zero))
    return rows

Result: partially reproduced. The tests hold: in V1 the cross projection does not lower d' (per population, all pairs: same 0.354 +/- 0.044, cross 0.380 +/- 0.039, p = 0.36), and in V4 it does (0.411 +/- 0.044 against 0.265 +/- 0.043, p = 0.0004; 18 degree pair 0.710 against 0.467, p = 0.002). The d' values are well below the paper's (0.95, 0.88, 1.02 and 0.67), under every reading. Per population, before averaging, the 18 degree pair gives same-axis d' of 0.02 to 1.66 in V1 and 0.08 to 1.36 in V4; 17 of 22 V1 populations are below 0.95 and 16 of 22 V4 populations below 1.02. Only 8 of 440 V1 and 7 of 440 V4 fixed decoders have no nonzero coefficient; replacing them changes the per-population means by at most 0.005 over all pairs (V1 same 0.359, V4 cross 0.263) and 0.008 for the 18 degree pair, and the tests give the same result (p = 0.43 and 0.0004).

Summary¶

A failure to reproduce here may be a failure of this attempt, not of the paper: see the reasoning and the differences from the paper's method.

How the analysis differs from the paper's. The paper's code is not public, so every method is the Methods' as the claims file reads them, with open details run under each reading. The decoders' penalty grid, z-scoring and fold assignment, the threshold-elevation grid, and the handling of zero means are standard choices stated in crowding.py. All deposited units are used, as the stated selection cannot be applied (data-populations). Noise correlations use every stimulus epoch, as the first epoch of a trial cannot be identified. Even and odd presentations follow the stored order, which for V4 is not the recording order; single random half splits keep about as many neurons as the stored-order split in both areas, and the tuning-model claims are repeated on a selection by reliability averaged over 20 random splits, under which fig5-terms-covary and fig5-terms-covary would not hold in V4, nor fig5de-simulated-discriminability under reading (a, a). Over 20 single random splits both hold in every split (fig5de against the selected neurons' own slopes), so the stored-order split is typical of the single split the paper describes. Under the stated penalty rule and the grid used here (lower bound C = 0.01) the chosen decoder has no nonzero coefficient in 5% to 18% of outer folds; replacing these decoders changes the threshold elevations little (V4 6.91 against 7.30 at 1.3 degrees) and the fixed-decoder d' by at most 0.008. With no crowding the threshold-elevation estimate is biased upward (1.17 in V1, 1.09 in V4), a property of the fit as the paper describes it; the permutation nulls are shifted further (V1 medians 1.37 to 1.63), so the V1 significance pattern depends on the null used.

What was found about the data set. (1) In sessions 1, 2 and 8 to 11 the epochs labelled blank and distractor-only respond as the target epochs do, so the spontaneous rate cannot be measured and the Methods' selection cannot be checked there. (2) V1 and V4 entries of the same population hold the same epochs but in different orders; the V1 order is consistent with the recording order and the V4 order is not, so epochs cannot be matched across areas and even/odd splits of V4 cannot follow time. 244 V4 units pass the reliability criterion against the paper's 198, while V1 gives the paper's 146 exactly; single random splits give similar counts (238 and 144 on average), so the order does not explain the difference. (3) The two epochs of a trial are not marked. (4) The files hold blank and distractor-only epochs and the spacing of the orientation experiment is not stored; the description mentions neither. (5) The receptive-field mapping, the per-session coarse mapping and the waveforms are not deposited.
